tasks.description: Given `s = '  Hello World  '`, strip the whitespace from both ends and print.
tasks.hint:
`.strip()` removes leading AND trailing whitespace (spaces, tabs, newlines).
It returns a new string — the original is unchanged.
`print(s.strip())` → `'Hello World'`
Also available: `.lstrip()` (left only) and `.rstrip()` (right only).
tasks.walkthrough:
`.strip()` removes whitespace from both ends and returns the trimmed copy.
The spaces in the middle between Hello and World are left alone.

tasks.description: Split the string 'apple,banana,cherry' by the comma and print the resulting list.
tasks.hint:
`.split(separator)` breaks a string into a list at each occurrence of the separator.
`'apple,banana,cherry'.split(',')` → `['apple', 'banana', 'cherry']`
Calling `.split()` with no argument splits on any whitespace.
tasks.walkthrough:
`.split(',')` breaks the string wherever there's a comma.
The result is a list of three strings, and printing a list shows the brackets and quotes.

tasks.description: Replace the word 'bad' with 'good' in 'Python is bad'. Print the result.
tasks.hint:
`.replace(old, new)` returns a new string with ALL occurrences of `old` changed to `new`.
`'Python is bad'.replace('bad', 'good')` → `'Python is good'`
Remember to print the result — the original string doesn't change.
tasks.walkthrough:
`.replace(old, new)` swaps every occurrence of the first string for the second.
It returns the new version, which goes straight into `print`.

tasks.description: Check if 'Hello, World!' starts with 'Hello'. Print the result (True or False).
tasks.hint:
`.startswith(prefix)` returns `True` if the string begins with the given prefix.
`'Hello, World!'.startswith('Hello')` → `True`
Companion method: `.endswith(suffix)` checks the end of a string.
tasks.walkthrough:
`.startswith()` checks the beginning of the string and returns a boolean.
Since the string does begin with Hello, the result is True.

tasks.description: Count how many times the letter 'l' appears in 'Hello, World!'. Print the count.
tasks.hint:
`.count(substring)` counts non-overlapping occurrences of the substring.
`'Hello, World!'.count('l')` → `3` (two in Hello, one in World)
Case-sensitive: `'l'` and `'L'` are counted separately.
tasks.walkthrough:
`.count()` tallies how many times the given text appears.
There are two l's in Hello and one in World, so 3.

tasks.description: Join the list ['Hello', 'World', 'Python'] into one string with a space between each word.
tasks.hint:
`.join(iterable)` is called on the separator, not the list — it's backward from what you'd expect.
`' '.join(['Hello', 'World', 'Python'])` → `'Hello World Python'`
The string before `.join()` is placed BETWEEN each item.
tasks.walkthrough:
The string before `.join` is the glue placed between each item.
A single space joins the three words into one sentence-like string.

tasks.description: Given `s = 'hello world'`, print it with the first letter of every word capitalised.
tasks.hint:
`.title()` capitalises the first letter of each word and lowercases the rest.
`'hello world'.title()` → `'Hello World'`
Alternative: `.split()` → capitalise each → `.join()`, but `.title()` is one step.
tasks.walkthrough:
`.title()` uppercases the first letter of every word and lowercases the rest.
It's one call, where the manual approach would be split, capitalise each word, then join.

lesson.intro:
Real data is messy text: extra spaces, wrong capitalisation, comma-separated
lists. Strings come with a toolkit of methods for cleaning and reshaping them.
Today is a tour of the ones you'll use over and over.

sections.heading: Methods return new strings
sections.body:
Every string method hands you back a new string. The original never changes.
If you want to keep the result, store it or print it.
sections.code:
s = '  Hello World  '
print(s.strip())
print(s.upper())
print(s.replace('World', 'There'))
print(s)
sections.output:
Hello World
  HELLO WORLD
  Hello There
  Hello World

sections.heading: Splitting text into pieces
sections.body:
`.split(',')` cuts the string at every comma and gives you a list of the
pieces. With no argument, it splits on any whitespace, which is the easy way
to get the words of a sentence.

sections.heading: Joining pieces back together
sections.body:
`.join()` is the reverse of split, and it's written back to front: the
separator comes first, then the list. Read `' '.join(words)` as
"join these words with a space".

sections.heading: Asking questions about a string
sections.body:
`.startswith()`, `.endswith()` and `in` give True or False.
`.count()` counts occurrences. `.find()` gives the position of the first
match, or -1 if it isn't there.
sections.code:
s = 'Hello, World!'
print(s.startswith('Hello'))
print(s.endswith('?'))
print(s.count('l'))
print(s.find('World'))

sections.heading: Changing case
sections.body:
`.upper()`, `.lower()`, `.title()` and `.capitalize()` each do one job.
`.title()` capitalises every word; `.capitalize()` only the first.

watch_out: Calling a method and forgetting the brackets: `s.upper` without `()` doesn't run anything.
`s.strip()` on its own line does nothing useful. Either print it or write `s = s.strip()`.
The separator goes before `.join`, not inside the brackets. `' '.join(words)`, not `words.join(' ')`.
`.count('l')` is case-sensitive, so it won't count `L`.
